usuario: Describe a protagonist in 100 to 150 words without mentioning any detail of their physical appearance (no clothes, height, eye or hair color): only through what they do and what they decide.
respuesta: She wakes before dawn every day, not from insomnia, but from the belief that the first hour belongs only to her. She fills the kettle twice, though she drinks only one cup, and sets the second on the windowsill for the neighbor's cat. When offered the promotion, she declines, choosing instead to train the new hire—not out of kindness, but because she remembers being lost and wants the maze to have fewer dead ends. She keeps a ledger of small debts: favors given, apologies owed, promises kept. In arguments, she listens without interrupting, then asks questions instead of offering rebuttals. Once a year, she burns letters she never sent, watching the smoke carry away versions of herself she decided not to become.

usuario: Choose an everyday, insignificant object and write a lyric poem of up to twelve lines that treats it as if it were an archaeological treasure or a historic monument.
respuesta:
Beneath the lamplight of this cramped museum shelf,
I excavate your silver spine, bent and half undone,
a reliquary of cellulose and rust,
each kink a hieroglyph of ten thousand Monday mornings.
You clipped, once, a note that spoke of distant harbors—
now you clasp nothing but the ghost of paper,
fossilized in iron oxide, precious as a scarab.
I catalog your patina, your elegant decay,
this humble helix that held the weight of words
before the digital age dissolved them into air.
How you glitter, artifact, outlasting the hand
that forged you, and every life you briefly held.

usuario: Write a tense scene of up to 150 words between two characters in which one interrogates the other without using a single question mark: they must get the information using only statements or psychological manipulation.
respuesta:
The door clicked shut. Marcus stood in the center of the room, his silhouette cutting the lamplight. Across from him, Elena pressed her back against the wall, fingers digging into the drywall.

"You think the darkness hides you." Marcus stepped closer, his shadow swallowing hers. "But I can smell the fear on you. Metallic. Coppery."

Elena swallowed. "There's nothing to tell."

"The safe combination sits in your left jacket pocket. I watched you check it this morning." He reached out, not touching, just hovering near her collarbone. "Tell me the numbers, or I start with your sister. She's alone at the house right now."

Her breath hitched. The silence stretched, thick and suffocating.

"Thirty-seven," she whispered. "Forty-two. Ninety-one."

Marcus smiled. "Good girl."

usuario: Write a conversation of up to 150 words between two people talking about something completely banal, while the reader understands perfectly that they are deciding the end of their relationship.
respuesta:
"Did you renew the parking sticker?"

"Expires next month. I’ll handle it."

"You sure? It’s under your name."

"Doesn’t matter. We’re selling the car anyway."

"Right. The Honda."

"Yeah. I already listed it."

"Okay. Good."

"Who’s keeping the couch?"

"I figured you’d want it. You bought it."

"Nah. You use it more."

"I’ll get a new one. Cheaper than moving it."

"Smart."

"Yeah."

"We should probably split the Netflix password then."

"Or just cancel it. Save the money."

"Good idea."

[They stand in the driveway, staring at the expired sticker.]

Exhumed from the sediment of drawer-strata,

still locked in devotion, one arm unfurled

usuario: Write a tense scene of up to 150 words between two characters in which one interrogates the other without using a single question mark: they must get the information using only statements or psychological manipulation.
respuesta:
"You want to talk about where you were last night." The interrogator's voice was flat, surgical. He set a photograph on the table — a girl, smiling, alive.

The suspect's eyes flicked to the image. A mistake.

"The lab already ran your shoe. Glass from the window matches." He leaned in. "You think silence protects you. It doesn't. It just tells me you have something to hide."

The suspect's jaw tightened.

"Right now, a jury sees a man who refused to cooperate. But if you tell me who else was in that house—" he paused, letting the silence thicken like blood—"I can make sure they understand you were forced into this."

A bead of sweat rolled past the suspect's temple.

"You're thinking about her mother. Whether she knows." The interrogator turned the photograph face-down. "Give me a name. Give me the truth. Let me help you survive what's coming."

The suspect's lips parted.

more lips than any chalice under glass,
has witnessed more confessions than the stones
of great cathedrals. Catalogue it: *beloved*.

"Warehouse on Calder Street. Tuesday night. You were seen."

Doyle folded his arms. "People see all kinds of things."

"Funny thing about your brother. He talked for two hours this morning. Gave us names. Dates." Marsh leaned back. "I'd hate to think he mentioned yours by mistake."

Doyle's jaw tightened. "Danny wouldn't."

"Danny did. But here's my problem—his story and the evidence don't quite match. Someone's lying, and the one who's lying takes the full sentence." Marsh tapped the photo. "Tell me about the shipment, and I'll assume the liar is him."

Silence stretched. The lamp buzzed.

"He's got kids," Doyle said finally, voice cracking.

"Then help him."

Doyle stared at his hands for a long moment. "The shipment comes in Friday. Pier nine. Midnight."

Marsh smiled. Danny hadn't said a word.

Mara counts the cutlery every night before locking the diner, not because anyone has ever stolen a fork, but because counting is how she tells herself the day is finished. When the regulars argue about the news, she refills their coffee and says nothing, then slips the quieter one an extra slice of pie. She has turned down three offers to sell the place, each time without explanation, though she keeps the letters in a drawer she opens on bad nights.

She pays her suppliers before she pays herself, forgives debts she never mentions, and has rehearsed exactly one apology for twenty years without delivering it. On Sundays, she drives to the cemetery and sits in the car with the engine running.

"You were at the warehouse on Thursday."

Reyes said nothing.

"Your wife thinks you were at your brother's. Your brother thinks you were at work. I've spoken to both. They're very fond of you. It would be a shame to put them in the same room."

"Marcus," he said. "The driver's name is Marcus. I only opened the gate."

Dvorak turned the photograph over. It was blank.

respuesta:
# Maya

Maya wakes before dawn to volunteer at the community kitchen, arriving before anyone else. She listens more than she speaks, remembering names and favorite meals from months prior. When a regular customer stops coming, she tracks them down and delivers soup to their apartment.

At her day job, Maya advocates loudly for fair wages her coworkers deserve, even when it complicates her standing with management. She donates half her raises anonymously to bail funds and education programs.

She makes mistakes—sometimes her empathy exhausts her, and she withdraws. She's been known to hold grudges. But she always apologizes, learns, and tries again.

Maya chooses the harder path consistently: confronting injustice, showing up for strangers, admitting when she's wrong. These choices have shaped her into someone her community trusts completely.

Behold this vessel, earthenware and worn,
Its glaze intact from some forgotten dawn,
A relic of a thousand careful mornings,
Where lips have pressed in ritual and longing.
The handle, smoothed by decades of devotion,
Bears the fingerprints of time's slow motion—
See how the chip along its rim declares
The violence of one careless moment spared,
Yet still it holds, still serves, still carries forth
The precious brew, more precious still for worth.
What civilizations rose and fell between
The first sip taken and this moment's sheen?

respuesta:
# The Confession

Detective Morgan leaned against the cold metal table, studying the suspect across from it.

"Your fingerprints are on the murder weapon," Morgan stated flatly. "We found them this morning."

Cole's jaw tightened. His fingers trembled slightly.

"The victim's blood matches the samples from your jacket," Morgan continued, stepping closer. "Your neighbor saw someone matching your description leaving the scene at 11:47 PM."

"I didn't—"

"You were there." Morgan's voice was ice. "We both know it. The only question now is whether you went there intending to kill, or if it was self-defense."

Cole's breathing quickened.

"Everyone understands self-defense," Morgan whispered, crouching beside him. "People sympathize with that. But premeditation... that's different. That's what prosecutors love."

Sweat beaded on Cole's forehead. His resolve crumbled.

"It was self-defense," he whispered.

Morgan smiled coldly.

"Thank you," she whispers, "for trying."

Victor slid the photographs across the metal table, leaving them face down. He didn’t need to flip them. The sweat beading on Silas’s upper lip told him everything. 

"You were the last one in the vault," Victor said, his voice a soft, flat drawl. "The ledger is gone. Your gambling debts are suddenly paid."

Silas stared at his own shaking hands. "I never touched it."

"Your wife thinks you're on a business trip," Victor continued, leaning in until the scent of his expensive cologne choked the stale air between them. "I can make that trip permanent. Or, you can give me an address. Right now."

Silas swallowed hard, his eyes darting to the locked door. 

"They won't protect you," Victor whispered. "I am the only one who can keep you breathing."

A heavy silence fell. Silas broke first. 

"Locker 42, Union Station." 

Victor smiled. "Good boy."

usuario: Choose an everyday, insignificant object and write a lyric poem of up to twelve lines that treats it as if it were an archaeological treasure or a historic monument.
respuesta:
**Ode to a Rusty Key**

Oh, relic of forgotten doors,
your teeth worn by time’s slow gnaw,
what secrets lie behind the jaws
you once unsealed with whispered lore?

A warder of wood, a guard of grain,
you turned in locks now turned to dust.
Yet still you bear the touch of hands
that trusted you—now lost, now rust.

What vaults did you, in prime, command?
What treasures slept beneath your sway?
Now just a weight in palm or pocket,
a silent keep of yesterday.

usuario: Write a tense scene of up to 150 words between two characters in which one interrogates the other without using a single question mark: they must get the information using only statements or psychological manipulation.
respuesta:
The dim light flickered as Daniel leaned in, his voice a low growl. "You know where the package is." His eyes locked onto hers, unblinking. "The boss won’t like it if you hold out on us."

Maria’s fingers tightened around her glass, knuckles white. "I don’t know what you’re talking about." Her voice wavered, just slightly.

Daniel smirked, dragging a chair across the floor with a screech. "Funny how you’re the only one who had access." He tapped his fingers on the table, slow, deliberate. "A person might think you’re hiding something."

Maria’s breath hitched. "I didn’t take anything."

"Then you won’t mind if we check your place." Daniel stood, looming over her. "Or maybe you’d rather tell me now and save everyone the trouble."

Her shoulders slumped, defeat creeping in. "Fine. It’s under the floorboards."

respuesta:
Nadia laid the burnt matchbook between them. “You always keep what you cannot bear to use.”

Corin did not blink.

“The warehouse had no witnesses, but grief talks. It writes checks, deletes cameras, leaves a car idling by the canal.”

He stared at the matchbook.

“If you stay silent, the report will call you the architect. Cold, efficient, proud.”

His lip twitched.

“I can also write that you tried to stop it. That you gave me a name.”

The room felt smaller.

“It wasn’t supposed to burn,” Corin said. “I only lit the office. The rest was Silas.”

“Should I leave my toothbrush in your cup?”

usuario: Describe a protagonist in 100 to 150 words without mentioning any detail of their physical appearance (no clothes, height, eye or hair color): only through what they do and what they decide.
respuesta:
**Mara**

Mara counts the exits in every room she enters, then sits with her back to the wall anyway, because her sister laughs easier when she can see the door. She keeps a list of people who owe her nothing and calls them on their birthdays. When the factory announced layoffs, she stayed late to teach the new hires the machines—knowing full well she was training her replacements. She once returned a lost wallet with the cash still inside, then lied to her friends and said she'd kept twenty. She signs petitions she doesn't fully understand and reads them afterward. Every April she plants tomatoes she knows the deer will eat. She votes. She tips too much. She apologizes to furniture when she bumps it. When asked why she bothers with any of it, she shrugs and says somebody has to.

usuario: Describe a protagonist in 100 to 150 words without mentioning any detail of their physical appearance (no clothes, height, eye or hair color): only through what they do and what they decide.
respuesta:
Mara keeps a list of everyone she's ever wronged, folded into her wallet like a confession she can't mail. Every Sunday she calls her grandmother, not out of duty, but because the old woman's laugh is the only sound that still makes her believe the world is repairable.

When a coworker takes credit for her work, Mara says nothing—then spends the night teaching herself the reporting software so thoroughly that no one can mistake whose mind is behind the numbers again. She believes in quiet competence over loud grievance.

At the grocery store, she always chooses the longest line, because the newest cashier needs someone patient. She quit her dream job once to care for her dying father, and though she never speaks of it, she measures every decision since against that year: if she could give that much, she can give more. Her greatest fear is not failure, but becoming someone who stops trying.

usuario: Choose an everyday, insignificant object and write a lyric poem of up to twelve lines that treats it as if it were an archaeological treasure or a historic monument.
respuesta:
**The Paperclip**

O twisted silver, coil of patient art,
unearthed from desk-dust, ancient as the morning—
what vanished hands once bent your shining heart,
what memos, gone to nothing, did you hold in keeping?

Scholars will debate your double loop,
your doctrine of soft custody, the way
you gripped without a wound, held fast, let go—
a civilization's genius: small, precise, and kind.

Museum glass will keep you now, coiled god
of order, relic of the paper age,
when words had weight, and needed, even then,
a humble spine of steel to hold them together.

usuario: Choose a complex feeling and define it in up to 120 words using only visual metaphors and textures, without ever using the word that names it. At the end, in square brackets, say which feeling it is.
respuesta:
A room where the walls are painted the color of almost-sunset, and the light can't decide whether to stay. It feels like velvet worn thin at the elbows—softness that has been touched too many times. There is a hummingbird's heartbeat in the chest of the room, wings beating against frosted glass. Everything is wrapped in slightly damp wool: heavy, warm, but never quite dry. Mirrors covered in breath-fog, showing shapes you recognize but can't name. The floor is made of honey—each step forward takes longer than it should and holds you gently in place. Threads of gold leaf crack across old ceramic, something broken becoming decoration. A held breath shaped like a paper lantern, glowing faintly, tethered by one silk string you're afraid to cut or pull closer.

[Longing]
razonamiento: Write ~120 words of visual/tactile metaphor.

respuesta:
**Sailing South**

Sam's small ship sank somewhere south. Swimming, Sam spotted sandy shores. Struggling, stormy seas swept seaweed sideways. "Survive!" Sam screamed, seizing soggy supplies floating past. Slowly, strength returned. Sandy beaches beckoned beautifully. Finally, Sam stood, shaking, soaking wet, smiling slightly. Six sunrises later, sailors spotted Sam's signal smoke, saving the stranded sailor. "Such splendid salvation!" Sam shouted, sailing safely seaward, seeking sunnier scenarios.

usuario: Write a tense scene of up to 150 words between two characters in which one interrogates the other without using a single question mark: they must get the information using only statements or psychological manipulation.
respuesta:
# The Ledger

Elena set the ledger on the table between them, letting the silence stretch until Marcus shifted in his chair.

"You were seen at the docks Tuesday night. Eleven forty." She tapped the leather cover. "The camera by the warehouse isn't as broken as your people believe."

Marcus laughed, thin and unconvincing. "I was home."

"Your wife says otherwise. She was quite cooperative this morning." Elena leaned back. "Funny thing about alibis—they unravel so quickly once someone starts pulling threads."

His jaw tightened. "She wouldn't—"

"She signed a statement. Eleven twenty to twelve thirty, you were gone." She slid a photograph across the table. "The man you met is telling us everything right now, in another room. He's getting a better deal by the minute. Yours shrinks every time I walk out that door."

The clock ticked. Marcus stared at the photo, then at his hands.

"Fine," he whispered. "It was Doren's money. But I never touched the girl."

Elena smiled and closed the ledger. "I know. I just needed you to say it."

usuario: Write a conversation of up to 150 words between two people talking about something completely banal, while the reader understands perfectly that they are deciding the end of their relationship.
respuesta:
**"The Kitchen Tap"**

"Drip's getting worse," Marianne said, not looking up.

"I noticed. Maybe it just needs a new washer."

"You said that in March."

"And it worked. For a while."

She ran her finger along the counter. "Some things aren't worth fixing, I suppose. When they get to a certain age."

"Everything can be fixed if you—" He stopped. "If someone wants to."

"Does anyone, though? Want to?"

The drip marked time. Plink. Plink.

"I could call someone tomorrow," he said. "A professional."

"Maybe that's better. Someone who isn't... emotionally invested in the faucet."

He almost laughed. Almost. "When?"

"Whenever. It's not urgent. Nothing's flooding."

"No. Just dripping. Constantly."

She finally looked at him. "There are boxes in the garage. From before."

"I know which ones you mean."

"Saturday, then. I'll be out by noon."

"I'll fix the tap after."

"Don't bother," she said softly. "You won't even hear it, soon."
razonamiento: Write subtext-laden banal dialogue.

She refused to charge admission, even when donations dwindled, believing stories should remain free for whoever needed them. When developers announced plans to demolish the building, she organized readings in the street, petitioned the council, and slept on the steps for nine nights to keep watch. usuario: Choose an everyday, insignificant object and write a lyric poem of up to twelve lines that treats it as if it were an archaeological treasure or a historic monument.
respuesta:
**O Paperclip, Gem of the Office Drawer**

How perfectly you've bent yourself for us,
your silver spine curved into a question
no one knows how to answer anymore.
I found you behind the desk, half-buried
in dust and the fossil husks of rubber bands,
still holding nothing, still committed—
little ark of a vanished attachment.

Who first folded you into this shape,
that does not grip or release but waits?
Your nested loops are nested centuries
of paper, of signatures, of small agreements
made between hands and forgotten by noon.
Hold me too, I whisper. Hold what is gone.
